comments.author: @phillipjacobs6808
comments.text:
People looking at this could be lead to believe that:-
1. living in the Grenadines is idyllic, which it is not. Food and other comser items are between 30-50% higher than on the mainland but salaries tend to be comparable.
2. Water is probable the most valuable commodity, and residents have to harvest rain.
3. Building a house there is conservatively twice the cost as on the mainland.
4. It's frustrating not to have small, usually easily available  items available
4. There are EIGHT inhabited Grenadine islands, not just the 3 mentioned. 
4. Mayreau (pronounced MY-ROW, as in row, row, row your boat), suffered as catastrophic damage as Union Island, but no mention was made of it or the residents there.
There are more shortcomings, but this is sufficient.
Full disclosure, I've lived on Mayreau for the last 37 YEARS, my children were born there, and I'm proud to call it home.

replies.author: @travellives
replies.text: We truly appreciate your perspective and for correcting the record on the number of inhabited islands and the specific impact of the hurricane on your community.

comments.author: @UnseenOutlands
comments.text: The recovery story of Union Island after Hurricane Beryl is one of the most moving parts of this documentary. Beyond rebuilding houses, how are families restoring their livelihoods, schools, and community spaces? What has been the biggest obstacle to recovery, and are local residents getting enough support to rebuild in ways that make their homes safer against future storms?

replies.author: @UnseenOutlands
replies.text: @travellives Nature remains an enigma that we humans cannot control.

replies.author: @travellives
replies.text: Families are restoring livelihoods through income support and business grants, while schools and services are being rebuilt with funding to improve resilience against future storms. ✨
